turns.question: Should a customer-facing reporting API query Snowflake directly or serve precomputed reporting data from Postgres?
turns.shown:
**Short answer:** For most customer-facing reporting APIs, serve precomputed data from Postgres, or from another serving layer. Don't point the API at a standard Snowflake warehouse. This is my judgment, not something a source states outright, and the assumptions below could change it. There is one real exception, covered further down.

**Why Postgres usually wins (my reasoning, backed by the sources)**
- **Cost shape.** Snowflake bills warehouses per second, with a 60-second minimum each time a warehouse starts or resumes [1]. A four-second query on a suspended warehouse costs a full minute. [1] Customer traffic is spread across the day, so you either keep a warehouse running or pay repeated resume minimums. Multi-cluster scaling adds to this. The rate is the warehouse's rate multiplied by the number of clusters running. [1]
- **Latency.** A suspended warehouse loses its cache. When a warehouse suspends, its local SSD cache is cleared, so the next start re-reads data from remote storage, which is slower. [2] A Postgres table with the right indexes doesn't have this cold-start behavior.
- **Predictability.** Snowflake's own guidance on concurrent app queries covers tuning concurrency settings and multi-cluster scaling. That is extra operational work for a workload that is usually simple lookups on precomputed rows.
- **Isolation.** If the API queries Snowflake directly, customer traffic competes with your analysts and pipelines, unless you give it a dedicated warehouse. Postgres keeps customer load off your analytics platform.

**The exception: Snowflake now has a purpose-built serving option**
- Snowflake's interactive tables and interactive warehouses are generally available and target low-latency, high-concurrency workloads such as data-powered APIs [3]. That went GA in December 2025.
- Since September 2026, interactive warehouses can query standard, dynamic, Iceberg and hybrid tables directly, without copying data into interactive tables [4].
- Snowflake's own example pairs Postgres for transactions with an interactive warehouse serving fast, concurrent analytical queries [5] on mirrored data.
- The trade-offs are cost and fit. Interactive warehouses are optimized to run continuously [6], so you pay for always-on compute. Per a third-party summary written at launch, they have a default 5-second timeout for SELECT queries [7]. I haven't checked whether that still holds, and the page was dated before the later zero-copy release. They also suit short, selective queries, so ad-hoc heavy aggregations are a poor fit. Snowflake also has hybrid tables, which it says can serve data directly at double-digit millisecond latency [8]. Most of this evidence is vendor material, so benchmark it yourself.

**How I'd decide**

| Your situation | Lean toward |
|---|---|
| Fixed set of reports, data refreshed hourly or daily, you already run Postgres | Postgres with precomputed tables |
| Customers need to slice by arbitrary filters or dimensions over large data | Snowflake interactive warehouse, or a dedicated OLAP engine |
| Data must be fresh within seconds | Snowflake interactive, or a streaming path into your serving store |
| Low or spiky traffic, no Postgres yet | Direct Snowflake on a dedicated warehouse, with resource monitors and timeouts, as a stopgap |
| Strict per-tenant security and a single governed source of truth | Snowflake's governance is a point in its favor. In Postgres you'd have to rebuild that access control. |

**If you go with Postgres**
- You take on a sync pipeline from Snowflake, a staleness window, and schema drift.
- Check that your aggregates can be precomputed. Postgres is much weaker than Snowflake at scanning large tables on demand.
- Show a "last updated" time in the API response.

**What I couldn't verify**
- I found no independent benchmarks or head-to-head cost comparisons. The interactive-warehouse performance claims come mostly from Snowflake and from blogs.
- Region availability and limits (timeouts, scaling behavior) change. Confirm them in the current Snowflake docs for your region and edition before committing.
- Your numbers would change the answer: requests per second, latency target, data volume per customer, freshness needed, and whether queries are fixed or ad hoc. If you share them, I can narrow this down.

Sources
[1] Snowflake Pricing in 2026: Credits, Warehouse Sizes, Storage and a Worked Bill — https://www.owox.com/blog/articles/snowflake-pricing-cost-control (search result age: 13 days ago)
[2] 8 best practices to reduce Snowflake costs (2026) — https://www.flexera.com/blog/finops/reduce-snowflake-costs/ (search result age: 68 days ago)
[3] Dec 11, 2025: Interactive tables and interactive warehouses (*General availability*) — https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2025/other/2025-12-11-interactive-tables-ga (search result age: 317 days ago)
[4] Sep 14, 2026: Zero-copy support for all table formats in interactive warehouses (*General availability*) — https://docs.snowflake.com/en/release-notes/2026/other/2026-09-14-interactive-zero-copy-ga (search result age: 40 days ago)
[5] Zero-Copy Interactive Analytics in Snowflake — https://www.snowflake.com/en/blog/engineering/zero-copy-interactive-analytics/ (search result age: 39 days ago)
[6] Getting Started with Snowflake Interactive Tables — https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/getting-started-with-interactive-tables/ (search result age: 354 days ago)
[7] Snowflake interactive tables and interactive warehouses — https://medium.com/@wondts/snowflake-interactive-tables-and-interactive-warehouses-f9a13547bcef (search result age: 313 days ago)
[8] Serving Low-Latency Data with Hybrid Tables — https://www.snowflake.com/en/developers/guides/hybrid-tables-serving-layer/ (search result age: 125 days ago)
